questions.text: Write the equation for the equilibrium occurring in a saturated solution of silver chloride, AgCl.

Calculate the solubility of AgCl in water at 25 degrees C, and give [Ag+] and [Cl-].

Ks(AgCl) = 1.70 x 10^-5
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct process. Merit: Correct solubility with units.

questions.text:
Below is a list of solutions available to add to a saturated solution of AgCl:

HCl(aq), NaBr(aq), NH3(aq), KNO3(aq)

Select and justify an appropriate solution to increase the solubility of AgCl.
questions.expectedAnswer: Add NH3. Ammonia forms a complex ion with Ag+, removing Ag+ from the equilibrium and shifting it forward, dissolving more AgCl.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises Ag+ can form a complex ion. Merit: Explains removal of Ag+ from equilibrium. Excellence: Full justification with equation.

questions.text: Select and justify an appropriate solution to decrease the solubility of AgCl.
questions.expectedAnswer: Add NaCl. Cl- is a common ion; increasing [Cl-] shifts equilibrium to the left (reverse), precipitating more AgCl.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises common ion. Merit: Explains shift to reverse.

questions.text:
Predict, by calculation, whether a precipitate of silver chloride, AgCl, will form when 30.0 mL of 0.0150 mol L-1 silver nitrate, AgNO3, is added to 20.0 mL of 0.0250 mol L-1 sodium chloride, NaCl.

Ks(AgCl) = 1.70 x 10^-5
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct [Ag+] OR [Cl-]. Merit: Correct process for IP. Excellence: Correct calculation and comparison.

questions.text:
List all the species present in a solution of sodium ethanoate, CH3COONa, in order of decreasing concentration. Do not include water.

Na+ > ___ > ___ = ___ > OH- > ___

Sodium ethanoate can be mixed with methanoic acid, HCOOH, to form a buffer solution.

Explain how this buffer solution would react upon the addition of a small volume of hydrochloric acid, HCl, including a balanced equation.
questions.expectedAnswer: When HCl is added, the basic component CH3COO- reacts with H3O+ to form CH3COOH, minimising pH change. CH3COO- + H3O+ -> CH3COOH + H2O
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies the acid is removed by the buffer. Merit: Explains the reaction with equation.

questions.text:
Calculate the mass of sodium ethanoate that must be added to 250 mL of 0.380 mol L-1 CH3COOH to give a buffer solution with a pH of 4.50.

Ka(CH3COOH) = 1.34 x 10^-5   pKa = 3.75   M(CH3COONa) = 96.1 g mol-1
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct substitution. Merit: Correct process with minor error. Excellence: Correct mass with units.

questions.text:
Three colourless 0.150 mol L-1 solutions of CH3NH2, CH3COOH, and (CH3NH3)Cl have lost their labels. The solutions are randomly labelled A, B, and C. The electrical conductivity of each solution, and the colour with bromothymol blue (pKa = 7.2), are shown.

Solution A: Poor conductivity, Yellow
Solution B: Poor conductivity, Blue
Solution C: Good conductivity, Yellow

Identify the three solutions. Justify your identification in terms of degree of dissociation and relative concentration of ions.
questions.expectedAnswer: A = CH3COOH (weak acid, poor conductivity, yellow = acidic). B = CH3NH2 (weak base, poor conductivity, blue = basic). C = (CH3NH3)Cl (fully dissociates, good conductivity, yellow = acidic salt).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises ions needed for conductivity. Merit: Links conductivity and colour for TWO solutions. Excellence: Justifies ALL THREE solutions.

questions.text:
A titration was carried out by adding 0.200 mol L-1 sodium hydroxide, NaOH, to 20.0 mL of 0.180 mol L-1 methanoic acid, HCOOH.

Ka(CH3COOH) = 1.34 x 10^-5   pKa = 3.75

Show, by calculation, that the initial pH of the propanoic acid solution is 2.45.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct substitution. Merit: Correct pH.

questions.text:
Sketch the missing portion of the titration curve between 0 and 17.5 mL to complete the curve provided.
Consider the initial pH, the pH after 10.0 mL of NaOH has been added, and the shape of the curve.
questions.expectedAnswer: The curve starts at the initial pH, gradually rises through the buffer region, then shows a steep rise near the equivalence point.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: At least ONE pH point plotted correctly. Merit: BOTH points plotted correctly with correctly drawn shape.

questions.text:
After a certain volume of NaOH has been added, the CH3COOH and CH3COONa are present in a 1:7 ratio.

Calculate the pH of this solution, and evaluate its buffering ability.
questions.expectedAnswer: pH = pKa + log(9/1) = 4.87 + 0.954 = 5.82. The buffer is more effective at neutralising added strong acid than strong base because there is much more conjugate base (9 parts) than acid (1 part).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct process. Merit: Correct pH and explanation. Excellence: pH and evaluation of buffer effectiveness.

questions.text:
Justify why the pH increases rapidly between 18.0 mL and 22.0 mL.
No calculations are necessary.
questions.expectedAnswer: Between 18 and 20 mL, the buffer becomes depleted as nearly all the propanoic acid has been neutralised. After 20 mL (equivalence point), excess NaOH is added directly, causing a rapid pH increase.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises the buffer is no longer effective. Merit: Explains the rapid pH increase near and past equivalence.

questions.text: Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.
questions.expectedAnswer: At equivalence, all CH3COOH has been converted to CH3COO-. The ethanoate ion hydrolyses: CH3COO- + H2O <=> CH3COOH + OH-. Kb = Kw/Ka = 1 x 10^-14 / 1.34 x 10^-5 = 7.46 x 10^-10. The resulting pH will be basic (around 8-9).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct process. Merit: Calculates pH but may not dilute correctly. Excellence: Correct pH at equivalence.

questions.text:
In a second titration, 20.0 mL of 0.180 mol L-1 methanoic acid, HCOOH, is titrated with the 0.185 mol L-1 NaOH solution.

Ka(HCOOH) = 1.77 x 10^-4   pKa = 3.75

Predict how the pH at the equivalence point will compare to the titration with propanoic acid.

    Lower pH        Same pH        Higher pH

Explain your choice.
questions.expectedAnswer: Higher pH. Ethanoic acid has a larger Ka than propanoic acid (1.74 x 10^-5 vs 1.34 x 10^-5), meaning it is a slightly stronger acid. Its conjugate base (ethanoate) is therefore a slightly weaker base, producing slightly less OH-... Actually: ethanoic acid has larger Ka so it is stronger, meaning its conjugate base is weaker, so less OH- produced, so lower pH. Wait - CH3COOH Ka = 1.74 x 10^-5 is larger than CH3COOH Ka = 1.34 x 10^-5. Larger Ka = stronger acid = weaker conjugate base = less hydrolysis = lower [OH-] = lower pH at equivalence. So answer is Lower pH.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises relative acid strengths. Merit: Links Ka to [OH-] at equivalence. Excellence: Correct prediction with full explanation.
